If prepare instead always generates a fresh ID whenever the final-block ID doesn't match a session's reservation, then re-running prepare on its own output would generate a second new random ID rather than recognizing its own stamp, causing a double trailer unless prepare persists that ID somewhere to recognize on re-entry.

However, the reviewer's request is narrower: restrict writes only to IDs prepare itself stamped, scoped to the post-commit side, leaving prepare's own behavior unchanged. That means a pasted or teammate-copied ID still links the commit in git terms, but post-commit refuses to write a checkpoint there — same as the existing "already in this clone" case where the commit ends up with no checkpoint at all.

This is consistent with how the tool already behaves when the ID exists locally, so extending the refusal to IDs that don't exist locally keeps things uniform, which is exactly what the reviewer wants. For the marker itself, I'm considering keeping the same trailers file but adding a `Stamped` field to the struct to record which checkpoint ID was stamped by prepare.

Mapping out the flow: at the point before stamping, I write or remove the marker depending on whether inherited trailers exist, then rewrite it with redone data in the redone-trailers path, and finally need a function to update the marker with the stamped checkpoint ID after stamping occurs, reading the existing marker if present or creating a new one with parents and the stamp if not.

To avoid redundant parent resolution, I'm considering reusing the marker's parents if it was just written this run, falling back to computing candidates only when the marker is absent -- which keeps the common no-inheritance path to a single cheap repository open rather than extra subprocess calls.

I also need to reconsider whether to clear the marker when nothing gets stamped, since the post-commit step relies on its absence to treat final-block IDs as foreign. There's an edge case where a prepare-stage marker lingers from an aborted commit (with Parents set to HEAD and HEAD^) -- the next prepare run on the same HEAD needs to either clear or overwrite that stale marker.

But a sequence operation like rebase or cherry-pick skips the prepare hook entirely and jumps straight to post-commit, so a stale marker could theoretically be consumed there. Since the stale Stamped value is always a fresh random token, it can only match a final block that already carries that same token, which only the originally prepared commit would have -- so stale markers can't cause an incorrect foreign match, even though cleaning them up proactively would still be tidier.

I also check the amend-restore path: the post-commit sees the session's LastCheckpointID in the final block, which exists locally and isn't in the marker's Stamped set, so it's treated as preexisting and only the owning session writes -- consistent with the existing rule. Similarly, for the amend-preserve path where the original trailer S still exists locally, it's handled correctly as preexisting, though I should check what happens if the original commit's post-commit never ran condensation in the first place.

I'm now considering a tricky edge case: if post-commit found no sessions for trailer S, then on amend with sessions present, S wouldn't exist locally and wouldn't be in marker.Stamped, so under the new rule it'd be foreign and sessions would refuse to write, leaving S dangling -- whereas today it would be treated as fresh and sessions would condense into it. This looks like a possible regression, so I need to check whether prepare reserves a PendingCondensationID for sessions in this scenario by looking more closely at `checkpointIDForSessions` and the surrounding logic in manual_commit_condensation.go.

I'm also tracing the redo path: if prepare returns before stamping, the marker only has inherited IDs and no new stamp, so post-commit sees nothing new and triggers reconcile correctly; with partial redo, a fresh S gets stamped after the inherited IDs, which also works as expected. Then I'm looking at the "entire attach" scenario, where attach amends the commit via `git commit --amend`, writing its new session ID into the checkpoint store before amending the message -- so by the time prepare runs, that ID already exists in the store.

I'm checking whether "attachJoinExisting" mode behaves the same way, since joining a commit just writes into the existing X without triggering amend, and post-commit treats it the same as any preexisting ID case, unaffected by my design changes. Now I'm considering edge cases like `--amend` on a commit whose fresh stamp came from prepare but where post-commit never actually ran.

Since `--no-verify` only bypasses pre-commit and commit-msg hooks, post-commit still executes, so S always gets condensed or refused during the same commit -- except if post-commit crashed, in which case the amend logic needs to check whether PendingCondensationID was set to S by prepare, since that would still satisfy the new rule. I'm now considering swapping in `strategy.FinalCheckpointTrailers` instead, but that pulls in a comment-prefix lookup from git config per commit, so I should hoist a shared trailer context via `strategy.WithCommentConfig` once rather than repeating the config read. There's also an earlier commit that seems to have intentionally made `--checkpoint` search match any ID, which could be relevant to the reviewer's second comment about `getAssociatedCommits`.

Thinking further, that earlier reasoning may stem from squash commits carrying checkpoints from their squashed children in the commit body—though a later commit moved inherited trailers into the final block, which should remove the need for body matching except for GitHub's "Squash and merge" commits, since those still embed the squashed messages directly in the body. That gap looks like the real justification for keeping the broader match.

I need to reconcile the single-commit view (CommitCheckpoint, which falls back to the first ID anywhere) with the listing view used by "explain X". For them to agree, a commit should count as associated with X if X appears in its final-block trailers, or if the final block is empty and X is the fallback ID found elsewhere in the message—I should check explain.go around lines 2460-2480 and 2820-2835, plus the 565f60b9e diff, to confirm this matches what the reviewer intended.

So the fix is to use "final block, else whole message" so that a commit with a final-block trailer for Y but a body mention of X shows up correctly under X, while still preserving GitHub's squash-merge discovery behavior. I'm considering a helper function that returns final checkpoint trailers if present, otherwise falls back to parsing all checkpoints in the body—though I want to check what the existing commit 565f60b9e did and its tests before deciding.

Now I'm wondering if there's already a checkpoint search function in explain.go around line 2827-2832 that uses this same final-trailers-with-fallback pattern, so I should look at that code before reimplementing.

content.content:
Adopting from a re-added source home drops the removed one's files. When
the marker can't be checked (a git or filesystem failure) the path rule
applies, so a transient error never stops the home linking; only a marker
that differs, or a missing one in the worktree's admin directory, counts as
proof for re-homing or dropping files. Turn-end recording (`homedAt`),
caller resolution's worktree tier, and status/review counts stay path-based:
they rely on turn start having followed or re-homed first. A sibling
worktree's hook that runs between a move and the moved home's next hook
still reads the stored transcript copy from the hook's own worktree.

**Only the final trailer block links a commit** (`stampedTrailer` in
prepare-commit-msg; `FinalCheckpointTrailers` in post-commit, attach, and
`explain --generate`). An `Entire-Checkpoint:` line anywhere else in the
message (pasted, quoted, indented, or mentioned in prose) names a checkpoint
the commit did not stamp, so prepare-commit-msg stamps a fresh trailer and
post-commit condenses there. Prepare judges the message it is handed by the
same rules, after applying git's cleanup, so it reads the final block
post-commit will read:

- **Grammar.** The block is read as git reads trailers: no leading
  whitespace, a key of letters, digits and dashes with optional spaces or
  tabs before its colon, indented lines only as continuations of a trailer,
  lines starting with git's comment prefix skipped (trailing ones too), and
  never the subject paragraph. Other lines are allowed only in a block
  holding a line git generates (`Signed-off-by: `,
  `(cherry picked from commit `), at most three per trailer line. Attach and
  `explain --generate` take the block's last ID.
- **Editor or not.** Git runs its commit hooks with `GIT_EDITOR=:` when it
  opens no editor (`-m`/`-F` without `-e`, `--no-edit`, `-C`). The source
  word cannot tell: `-m -e` reports `message`, and an amend reports `commit`
  either way. A `GIT_EDITOR=:` the user exports looks the same, so such a
  commit is treated as one git does not open: its trailer goes after git's
  comment block (below the diff with `-v`, where git discards it), and a
  message saved untouched is recorded holding only the trailer instead of
  aborting.
- **Cleanup.** A message git opens loses the lines starting with git's
  comment prefix and everything from the exact scissors line down; any other
  message keeps its comment lines, which git's trailer grammar still skips.
  `commit.cleanup=strip` drops comment lines from every message, and
---345-425---
  anywhere only when the final block names none. `explain --checkpoint`
  finds every commit that names the checkpoint anywhere. Other read-only
  lookups (resume, status, attribution, other history listings) still scan
  the whole message, because squash commits carry their squashed commits'
  trailers in the body.
- **Inheritance.** Squash and redo inheritance take their IDs from the whole
  message of SQUASH_MSG and of the redone commits, for the same reason, and
  add each to the final block unless it is already there: a copy indented in
  the body, as git seeds an editor squash message, does not count.
- **Writer.** The trailer writer joins the final paragraph when it is a
  trailer block read without a comment prefix, the strictest reading, so
  every reader accepts the trailer it appends and a mixed block keeps its
  trailers in the final block. Any other paragraph gets the trailer in a new
  block.

**Squashes inherit their trailers** (`inheritSquashedCheckpointTrailers`). A
commit made while `git merge --squash` is in progress (SQUASH_MSG present in
the per-worktree git dir) contains the squashed commits' work, so every
`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer in SQUASH_MSG is carried into the message's
final block when missing there, when a staged path is one a commit Git
recorded there changed; a file
touched up before committing still counts. An abandoned squash can leave
SQUASH_MSG behind; staged work on other paths therefore inherits nothing, and inherited trailers in Git's seeded message are
removed. git only reports source `squash` when its seeded message is accepted;
a squash committed with `-m` reports `message`, which used to run ordinary
matching and either refuse or mint a fresh, empty checkpoint. Inherited
trailers are links to checkpoints that already exist. Matching still runs, so
work a session holds at squash time is stamped as its own trailer after the
inherited ones, and post-commit condenses only into the trailer that has no
checkpoint yet (`pickCondensationTarget`) among those prepare stamped: prepare
records the inherited IDs in the per-worktree git dir, tied to the commit's
parent (`recordInheritedTrailers`), so an inherited trailer whose checkpoint
simply is not in this clone's store yet is never mistaken for a fresh one, rechecks whether that target appeared
between selection and condensation, and never writes into an inherited one; a
write into a checkpoint the session did not stamp for this commit is refused
(`stampedByAnotherCommit`). Merge commits stay unlinked by design; the
merged commits keep their own trailers.

**Redone commits inherit their trailers too** (`inheritReplacedCommitsTrailers`).
After `git reset` and new commits, the dropped commits are read from HEAD's
reflog, not ORIG_HEAD (which unstaging or a stash overwrites): walking back from
the newest entry, resets that did not move HEAD are skipped, and the tip the
last real reset left is where the dropped work starts. Dropped means only that
tip reaches it: commits HEAD, a remote or another branch still reach (merged-in
main, a teammate's commit an undone rebase brought in) are never inherited,
while a backup branch pointing at the tip itself does not count. A dropped
commit's trailers are carried into the new message when every staged file it
changed has exactly the content it had at that tip (read from the index git is
preparing the commit in, so `git commit -a` and path-limited commits compare
what they commit), so an agent's ten commits
redone as three logical ones keep every checkpoint, each on the commit that now
holds its files, while one coincidentally identical file (a lockfile, an empty
`__init__.py`, the same deletion) among rewritten ones inherits nothing. Commits
made since the reset keep the redo open only while each of them redid some of
the dropped work; any other ref operation (checkout, merge, rebase, pull) ends
it. Folding with `git reset --soft HEAD~1 && git commit --amend` inherits the
folded commit's trailers too. Inherited trailers are links, exactly as for a
squash, and are recorded so post-commit never condenses into one. Unlike a
squash, the staged files a redo inherited for are no evidence of new session
work: the reset put them back in the worktree and the next turn end records
them as touched again, though the session did nothing new to them. A staged
path counts as held only when the newest dropped commit that changed it
carries a checkpoint this clone has (a trailer whose capture failed still
links, but holds nothing) and the staged mode matches too. Session matching
ignores held paths, so a commit that only redoes linked work gets no fresh
trailer, and one that also stages other session work gets one for that work.
Session matching reads the same rename-free staged paths the redo compared.
Prepare records the held paths beside the inherited IDs. After a redo that
stamps nothing and so condenses nothing, post-commit drops them from
the touched files of this worktree's sessions when the commit holds the
recorded content, as carry-forward would; other touched files, steps and
transcript growth stay pending. When a fresh trailer is stamped, post-commit
judges overlap without the redo, so a session that only redid work may fold
into it: that keeps every stamped trailer resolvable (a stale ACTIVE or a
read-only session can depend on it). The mid-turn agent fast path likewise
still stamps on a partial redo: transcripts miss edits made through shell
commands, so it cannot rule new work out. In both, a redundant checkpoint is
preferred to a lost or dangling link.

**Worktree matching** (always computed; the sole mechanism for commits with
no recorded agent in their ancestry — human commits, detached runners): exact

Adopting from a re-added source home drops the removed one's files. When
the marker can't be checked (a git or filesystem failure) the path rule
applies, so a transient error never stops the home linking; only a marker
that differs, or a missing one in the worktree's admin directory, counts as
proof for re-homing or dropping files. Turn-end recording (`homedAt`),
caller resolution's worktree tier, and status/review counts stay path-based:
they rely on turn start having followed or re-homed first. A sibling
worktree's hook that runs between a move and the moved home's next hook
still reads the stored transcript copy from the hook's own worktree.

**Only the final trailer block links a commit** (`stampedTrailer` in
prepare-commit-msg; `FinalCheckpointTrailers` in post-commit, attach, and
`explain --generate`). An `Entire-Checkpoint:` line anywhere else in the
message (pasted, quoted, indented, or mentioned in prose) names a checkpoint
the commit did not stamp, so prepare-commit-msg stamps a fresh trailer and
post-commit condenses there. Prepare judges the message it is handed by the
same rules, after applying git's cleanup, so it reads the final block
post-commit will read:

- **Grammar.** The block is read as git reads trailers: no leading
  whitespace, a key of letters, digits and dashes with optional spaces or
  tabs before its colon, indented lines only as continuations of a trailer,
  lines starting with git's comment prefix skipped (trailing ones too), and
  never the subject paragraph. Other lines are allowed only in a block
  holding a line git generates (`Signed-off-by: `,
  `(cherry picked from commit `), at most three per trailer line. Attach and
  `explain --generate` take the block's last ID.
- **Editor or not.** Git runs its commit hooks with `GIT_EDITOR=:` when it
  opens no editor (`-m`/`-F` without `-e`, `--no-edit`, `-C`). The source
  word cannot tell: `-m -e` reports `message`, and an amend reports `commit`

  comment block (below the diff with `-v`, where git discards it), and a
  message saved untouched is recorded holding only the trailer instead of
  aborting.

  comment prefix and everything from the exact scissors line down; any other
  message keeps its comment lines, which git's trailer grammar still skips.
  `commit.cleanup=strip` drops comment lines from every message, and
---345-425---
  anywhere only when the final block names none. `explain --checkpoint`
  finds every commit that names the checkpoint anywhere. Other read-only
  lookups (resume, status, attribution, other history listings) still scan
  the whole message, because squash commits carry their squashed commits'
  trailers in the body.
- **Inheritance.** Squash and redo inheritance take their IDs from the whole
  message of SQUASH_MSG and of the redone commits, for the same reason, and
  add each to the final block unless it is already there: a copy indented in
  the body, as git seeds an editor squash message, does not count.
- **Writer.** The trailer writer joins the final paragraph when it is a
  trailer block read without a comment prefix, the strictest reading, so
  every reader accepts the trailer it appends and a mixed block keeps its
  trailers in the final block. Any other paragraph gets the trailer in a new

**Squashes inherit their trailers** (`inheritSquashedCheckpointTrailers`). A
commit made while `git merge --squash` is in progress (SQUASH_MSG present in
the per-worktree git dir) contains the squashed commits' work, so every
`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer in SQUASH_MSG is carried into the message's
final block when missing there, when a staged path is one a commit Git
recorded there changed; a file
touched up before committing still counts. An abandoned squash can leave
SQUASH_MSG behind; staged work on other paths therefore inherits nothing, and inherited trailers in Git's seeded message are
removed. git only reports source `squash` when its seeded message is accepted;
a squash committed with `-m` reports `message`, which used to run ordinary
matching and either refuse or mint a fresh, empty checkpoint. Inherited
trailers are links to checkpoints that already exist. Matching still runs, so
work a session holds at squash time is stamped as its own trailer after the
inherited ones, and post-commit condenses only into the trailer that has no
checkpoint yet (`pickCondensationTarget`) among those prepare stamped: prepare
records the inherited IDs in the per-worktree git dir, tied to the commit's
parent (`recordInheritedTrailers`), so an inherited trailer whose checkpoint
simply is not in this clone's store yet is never mistaken for a fresh one, rechecks whether that target appeared
between selection and condensation, and never writes into an inherited one; a
write into a checkpoint the session did not stamp for this commit is refused
(`stampedByAnotherCommit`). Merge commits stay unlinked by design; the
merged commits keep their own trailers.

**Redone commits inherit their trailers too** (`inheritReplacedCommitsTrailers`).
After `git reset` and new commits, the dropped commits are read from HEAD's
reflog, not ORIG_HEAD (which unstaging or a stash overwrites): walking back from
the newest entry, resets that did not move HEAD are skipped, and the tip the
last real reset left is where the dropped work starts. Dropped means only that
tip reaches it: commits HEAD, a remote or another branch still reach (merged-in
main, a teammate's commit an undone rebase brought in) are never inherited,
while a backup branch pointing at the tip itself does not count. A dropped
commit's trailers are carried into the new message when every staged file it
changed has exactly the content it had at that tip (read from the index git is
preparing the commit in, so `git commit -a` and path-limited commits compare
what they commit), so an agent's ten commits
redone as three logical ones keep every checkpoint, each on the commit that now
holds its files, while one coincidentally identical file (a lockfile, an empty
`__init__.py`, the same deletion) among rewritten ones inherits nothing. Commits
made since the reset keep the redo open only while each of them redid some of
the dropped work; any other ref operation (checkout, merge, rebase, pull) ends
it. Folding with `git reset --soft HEAD~1 && git commit --amend` inherits the
folded commit's trailers too. Inherited trailers are links, exactly as for a
squash, and are recorded so post-commit never condenses into one. Unlike a
squash, the staged files a redo inherited for are no evidence of new session
work: the reset put them back in the worktree and the next turn end records
them as touched again, though the session did nothing new to them. A staged
path counts as held only when the newest dropped commit that changed it
carries a checkpoint this clone has (a trailer whose capture failed still
links, but holds nothing) and the staged mode matches too. Session matching
ignores held paths, so a commit that only redoes linked work gets no fresh
trailer, and one that also stages other session work gets one for that work.
Session matching reads the same rename-free staged paths the redo compared.
Prepare records the held paths beside the inherited IDs. After a redo that
stamps nothing and so condenses nothing, post-commit drops them from
the touched files of this worktree's sessions when the commit holds the
recorded content, as carry-forward would; other touched files, steps and
transcript growth stay pending. When a fresh trailer is stamped, post-commit
judges overlap without the redo, so a session that only redid work may fold
into it: that keeps every stamped trailer resolvable (a stale ACTIVE or a
read-only session can depend on it). The mid-turn agent fast path likewise
still stamps on a partial redo: transcripts miss edits made through shell
commands, so it cannot rule new work out. In both, a redundant checkpoint is
preferred to a lost or dangling link.

**Worktree matching** (always computed; the sole mechanism for commits with
no recorded agent in their ancestry — human commits, detached runners): exact

I need to verify this is correct for the case like `-C teammate-sha` with an unfetched commit — the amend path preserves it, nothing gets minted, and since it doesn't exist in the store, there's no target, so only BaseCommit gets updated while the session's pending work isn't condensed. I should check that this path doesn't accidentally drop that pending work rather than carrying it forward.

The amend path's restore logic only stamps LastCheckpointID for sessions where BaseCommit equals HEAD, and it never does content detection to stamp fresh trailers for new work — so for `-C teammate-sha`, not writing into that trailer is consistent and our work correctly stays pending. For the `-m` case where a trailer is pasted into the source message, that goes through the slower stamping path instead.

Since X isn't minted or session-owned, it won't register as "already stamped," so prepare mints a fresh trailer Y, giving a chain of [X, Y] with Y recorded as minted and targeted post-commit. I'm also considering edge cases: if the minted-record write fails (best-effort) after prepare stamps Y, the fallback to "last trailer without checkpoint" might find nothing, leaving work uncondensed and Y dangling — degraded but safe, matching the old behavior where the store-unavailable fallback just uses wherever prepare stamped last. And then there's the squash scenario with inherited trailers X1, X2, plus a newly minted one to work through.

Also if a crash happens mid-commit before post-commit runs, the next prepare would mint another id and minted would accumulate both, but post-commit still picks the last one in the final block, so that's fine.

Comparing replace vs append semantics, I realize replace has an edge case where an interleaved aborted attempt's ID gets overwritten before its retry can use it — acceptable but worth noting. Append avoids that by preserving minted-but-unused IDs, at the cost of one extra read; I'll lean toward append with dedupe since it's conceptually cleaner for reviewers to reason about.

I'm also checking whether concurrent prepare-commit-msg runs could race within a worktree, but since git holds index.lock during commit, that's not a concern. Now I'm considering how the stamped trailer should be validated: an ID should be accepted if it's either in the minted set or already owned by a session's tracked state.

For amend cases where X is already owned by a session, stamping without session vouching would mint a new Y and link both X and Y, whereas vouching keeps X stable and lets post-commit condense into X via the owner guard — both are safe, but vouching stays closer to current behavior. I also need to double-check whether the slow path's stampedTrailer function would need a sessions parameter added, since it currently doesn't take one.

I'm now worried existing tests pin the "trailer already exists" skip behavior with arbitrary non-minted, non-owned X values in the message, expecting prepare to leave them untouched — my change would break those tests, which is actually the exact bug #1 is meant to fix, so I'll need to update them. Let me reconsider whether changing prepare's keep-decision is even necessary, since the post-commit guard alone might already resolve #1.

Actually, stamping fresh after a foreign X does help, since it links the work rather than leaving it pending, and it also addresses #9's concern about prepare and post-commit disagreeing — if prepare mints a record, post-commit can use it and they'll agree. But if prepare keeps a foreign X without stamping, post-commit falls back to "last existing," which for an unfetched pasted X leaves work pending, and for a fetched/existing X triggers the owner guard refusal — matching the PR's own description of a commit ending up with no checkpoint at all, which is exactly what this PR claims to fix.

So I'm leaning toward having prepare stamp fresh whenever the final-block ID isn't vouched for, to keep behavior consistent with the PR's goal. That raises the question of how "vouched" works here — it needs session-ownership checks, so I need to see where `stampedTrailer` is called: the slow path passes `sessions` and `sessionsWithContent`, while the fast path passes a single `state` plus `provenance.withoutForeign(sessions)`. I think I should pass along whatever sessions are available in each path, since ownership just means any session in this worktree/clone matches.

I'm also second-guessing whether vouching via LastCheckpointID is actually safe in prepare for a scenario where session S's LastCheckpointID = X already exists and is its own.

Tracing through: if someone does a new (non-amend) commit pasting their own prior checkpoint X as the trailer, prepare keeps X since it's vouched, and post-commit mints an empty value, finds the last existing X, and since the owner guard matches (S.LastCheckpointID == X), it condenses S's new work into X — so two commits end up linking to X with new work appended. That matches what main already does, so it's acceptable and unchanged.

For the `--amend -m` case with an existing X: if there's no new content since the last condensation, prepare returns early without stamping anything, X stays as-is, and post-commit's owner-guard condensation is essentially a no-op. So the real case where vouching matters is `--amend -m` when X is present but there's actual new content to consider.

Without session vouching, amending would end up keeping both X and a newly minted Y with the new work folded into Y, whereas the existing codebase's amend behavior folds everything back into X so the checkpoint identity stays stable across the amend. To stay consistent with that expectation, I'll keep the session vouching mechanism (LastCheckpointID/Pending) — it's a small addition.

I'm also second-guessing whether there's a simpler framing a reviewer would accept, something like "post-commit only ever writes into a final-block ID that prepare itself stamped, and prepare/post-commit agree on that." I think the current design holds up, so now I'm turning to the agent fast path: tryAgentCommitFastPath calls addTrailerForAgentCommit, which returns early if a stamped trailer is already found, and otherwise mints a new checkpoint ID, writes it, and records it as minted.

Then there's the amend-restore path, where the restored LastCheckpointID is normally owned and already exists — I'm checking whether recording that as "minted" works cleanly with post-commit's target resolution, preexisting flag, and the owner guard that checks whether the session's LastCheckpointID matches it, which should allow that session to proceed.

I'm now thinking the recording isn't strictly required since the fallback "pick the last existing ID" would catch it anyway, but recording it still makes target selection exact, so I'll keep it — just renaming the concept from "minted" to "stamped" (i.e., "IDs that prepare-commit-msg wrote into a message") to better match the semantics. The post-commit guard then only allows a non-preexisting target if it was stamped, and for a restored LastCheckpointID that isn't deleted but also isn't tracked as existing, being stamped means it's still ours and safe to create.

Now I'm rewriting the per-session guard function itself — adjusting `stampedByAnotherCommit` to take the checkpoint ID and session state, returning false immediately if the ID matches the session's current LastCheckpointID or its pending condensation ID, and otherwise checking context flags for whether the target was preexisting or unstamped.

I'm now testing whether this guard still needs extra logic given a possible race: prepare reserves a pending condensation ID for a session, but eager condensation at session stop could condense that same ID before post-commit runs, making it preexist by the time the guard checks ownership — I want to confirm existing behavior (checking if Pending matches) already handles this correctly for both the owning and other sessions. I'm concluding that since target selection now guarantees any non-preexisting target must be stamped, the per-session ownership guard doesn't need further changes — the target selection logic (case 1: last stamped ID with preexisting check, case 2: fallback when nothing is stamped) already does the necessary work.

The localized change is just that prepare now records stamped IDs, which `stampedTrailersOf` and `condensationTarget` use, with prepare's `stampedTrailer` vouching for them. I'm also checking this doesn't break existing provenance tests, like the amend-of-squash scenario, and considering edge cases like store-open failures where preexisting can't be determined.

Reasoning that stamped IDs are always ours since a foreign ID can never enter the stamped list unless prepare's vouching explicitly recorded it, and prepare's keep path doesn't record anything — only minting does. Squash inheritance writes inherited IDs separately, which post-commit already filters out, and with vouching via the stamped list, running the hook twice just keeps the state consistent.

Now I'm worried about tests that fabricate commits with a handcrafted checkpoint trailer and call PostCommit directly without running prepare first — those would never get stamped, so under the new logic they'd fall into the "ID doesn't exist" case and fail to condense. I need to grep for this pattern across the strategy test suite to gauge how many tests would break, since integration tests that actually run git commit should be fine but unit tests calling PostCommit directly are the risk.

I'm also tracing through the checkpoint-matching logic for getAssociatedCommits, which currently parses the whole commit message rather than just the final trailer block. For squash commits created by Entire itself, inherited checkpoint IDs land in the final trailer block so FinalCheckpointTrailers would catch them, but GitHub's "Squash and merge" default commit body lists each squashed commit's subject and trailers unindented in the body, which complicates whether those IDs would still be found if I restrict matching to the final block.

Comparing against main's behavior: previously getAssociatedCommits used ParseCheckpoint, which just grabs the first checkpoint ID anywhere in the message, so for a GitHub squash merge with multiple checkpoint trailers, only the first one (e.g. X1) would match. Switching to FinalCheckpointTrailers changes this — now only the ID in the final trailer block (likely the last commit's, X3) would match, meaning X1 lookups that worked on main would stop working under the new approach. That's a real regression I need to account for.

To fix this and stay consistent with how CommitCheckpoint already works (final block, falling back to first-anywhere only when the final block is empty), getAssociatedCommits should match if X is in the final trailer block, or — only when that block names nothing — fall back to matching X against the first ID anywhere via ParseCheckpoint. This mirrors the existing fallback logic exactly and should satisfy the reviewer's concern about body lines like "Follow-up to..." style references.

Following the reviewer's suggestion strictly would actually break GitHub's squash-merge first-commit discovery behavior and diverge from how CommitCheckpoint's fallback is documented, so that's a real tension worth flagging rather than just complying.

Writing fallback logic...

Also need to set up the comment config context once for the walk, since the fallback trailer lookup may need git config per commit when the strict read misses but the message still contains the key.

There's also a subtlety with the fallback that lists the first ID anywhere when the final block names none — in the reviewer's example, a commit lacking a final-block trailer would still get listed under the PR's read-only fallback, and I think that's defensible since both views end up agreeing on the same commit.

But the strict option risks someone noticing a disagreement between explain and the listing for commits without a final block — which is exactly the inconsistency that an earlier fix addressed, where explain showed one commit but the listing showed another and checking by checkpoint found nothing.

I'll go with reusing CommitCheckpoint's rule for consistency, structuring the code so both paths share one function. I'm planning tests: a commit with final block Y but body mentioning X should fail on `--checkpoint X` but succeed on Y, while a commit with no final block should find X anywhere in the body, matching explain's behavior — and for squash commits with multiple checkpoints in the final block, checking any of them should still find the commit.

Now I'm turning to issue #3: whether squash and redo inheritance should treat body mentions as real links. IDs get collected across the whole squash/redo message and written into the final block, but the reviewer flagged this as a documented gap. For redo, replaced commits' checkpoint links follow the same final-block rule, so body-only mentions in those replaced commits shouldn't be inherited — though I need to consider the case where a replaced commit was itself a squash commit.

Now I'm thinking through the SQUASH_MSG format git generates for `git merge --squash`, which lists each squashed commit with its author, date, subject, body, and trailer block in sequence.

Since these are indented by four spaces, trailers embedded there aren't "final block" in the normal grammar sense. The better approach is to use the existing logic that already parses `commit <sha>` lines from SQUASH_MSG and loads those commit objects — I can reuse that to look up each commit's actual recorded message and extract its final checkpoint trailers directly, which is more precise than trying to parse the indented text.

This also depends on confirming SQUASH_MSG is only produced by `git merge --squash` (not interactive rebase, which writes to a different file), so the `commit <sha>` header format should be reliable across cases.

I'm trying to recall whether git's squash message revision walk actually reverses order to produce oldest-first output, since the redo code's comment claims "oldest first, like a squash message" but my memory of merge.c's default walk suggests newest-first unless there's an explicit reverse flag.

Regardless, I decide to just preserve SQUASH_MSG's textual order by walking its "commit <sha>" header lines sequentially, matching the order ParseAllCheckpoints already produces. This means inheritSquashedCheckpointTrailers needs restructuring: it currently computes the inherited set before opening the repo, but now it needs repo access first since squashTouchesStagedPath already opens it — though the common non-squash case still short-circuits early since SQUASH_MSG won't exist then.

If a listed commit can't be loaded, I'll just skip it and inherit nothing from it rather than falling back to text parsing, since these commits were just merged and should normally be accessible. For stripInheritedCheckpointTrailers, I'm checking whether the new inherited computation still works correctly with the whole-line trailer match after TrimSpace — the stale-SQUASH_MSG strip should still remove indented trailer lines seeded by the editor flow, while leaving body-text mentions of checkpoint IDs untouched since those are just prose and not functional links.

I think this squash fix is reasonable to make since it closes a documented gap and is fairly contained, though I want to check manual_commit_squash_test.go first to see how existing tests construct SQUASH_MSG and whether they rely on fake commit SHAs or inline trailer text that this change might break.

For the redo path, I'm checking whether it correctly parses checkpoint trailers from the replaced commits' messages, keeping in mind those could be old-style squash commits with body trailers, and whether redo might end up inheriting from a replaced commit that's itself part of a chain.

Now I'm digging into issue #4: how git config's `--get-regexp` prints keys with and without values for boolean settings like `commit.status`. The current parsing logic using `strings.Cut` on space ends up treating an empty value as true when it should be false, since git treats an empty string after the key as false but a truly valueless key as true -- the code conflates these two cases.

Numeric parsing with unit suffixes like "0k" would still resolve to zero, so that edge case is fine. I don't want extra spawns just to resolve bool-type config separately, so the better fix is to split the line into key and value while tracking whether a value was present at all, then treat a missing value as true and otherwise evaluate it against the standard true/false/yes/no/on/off tokens.

Since git itself dies on unparseable commit.status values anyway, I don't need to be exhaustive here — the reviewer only flagged the empty-value case, so I'll keep the fix narrow: handle no-value, explicit false-like strings, and integers, wrapping it into a small helper function.

I'm also considering git's commit.status override behavior via --status/--no-status flags, which isn't handled here—a documented gap. For testing, I'm thinking I'd need a case setting commit.status to empty string versus valueless in a temp repo to verify the resulting config, though AGENTS.md's guidance against writing unit tests after production code means I should focus on enumerating failure modes instead.

The best approach is probably adding a row to the real-git matrix test with `commit.status=` empty and `core.commentChar=auto`, since the actual failure is that guessing the comment prefix without a real block can diverge from what git picks, leaving explanation lines unstripped and triggering a spurious prompt. An end-to-end test through actual git commits would catch this more convincingly than a mocked unit test.

Separately, I'm noting another bug to investigate next: HasOPFApplied returning false for a trailer-only message.

Tracing finalTrailerBlock, since start==0 is rejected as the subject paragraph, a commit message with just "Entire-OPF-Applied: true" alone ends up with HasOPFApplied false, causing pre-push to redact again. Tracing AppendOPFAppliedTrailer against an empty oldCommit.Message, appendTrailerLine produces a single blank line, which trips the separated flag early and leaves isTrailerBlock seeing an empty slice, so it returns false and the result collapses to an empty string.

The result becomes "\n\nEntire-OPF-Applied: true\n", and re-running HasOPFApplied on that reconstructed message now correctly identifies start=2, satisfying isTrailerBlock since start isn't 0. So the empty-message round trip actually works fine through go-git, since messages are encoded verbatim.

Now I need to figure out when a message could end up truly trailer-only, which points me back to checking what v1 checkpoint commit messages actually look like.

I need to check whether main's HasOPFApplied scanned all lines for the trailer key rather than requiring it in the final paragraph, since that's the only way a message consisting solely of "Entire-OPF-Applied: true" would have passed before. The reviewer's point is that this edge case now fails the subject-paragraph check, causing pre-push to redact a commit that already carries the trailer.

I think the real fix is that HasOPFApplied shouldn't inherit the subject-line exemption rule from finalTrailerBlock, since OPF messages are machine-written rather than user commits. I'm considering splitting finalTrailerBlock into a helper that optionally skips the subject check, so OPF detection can use a variant that treats the whole message as trailer-eligible when appropriate.

I should check git log to see how HasOPFApplied evolved in this branch.

There's also a design concern worth considering: reimplementing git's trailer/cleanup rules instead of using `git interpret-trailers --parse` for recorded commits. Switching post-commit/attach/explain to that approach would add a git spawn per read, which could get costly when explain walks many commits—though batching might help. Prepare would still need Go logic since it parses an unrecorded message before cleanup is applied.

Changing the reader architecture now is too large a scope expansion and would invite more review. I think the better move is addressing this in the PR description with a short rationale rather than code: the real guard against git version mismatches is the real-git matrix test pinned to specific versions in CI, not a rewrite of the reader logic.

I could also consider whether `git interpret-trailers --parse` could serve as the authoritative reader for already-recorded commits in post-commit, but that adds an extra spawn per commit and doesn't cleanly capture the "final block" semantics I need, so it's not a clear win within scope.

For #7, the concern about having a second git --version parser could be resolved by having strategy reuse telemetry's gitVersion/parseGitVersion, but those are unexported, so I'd need to decide whether exporting them from the telemetry package makes sense given its purpose.

Alternatively, I could centralize this in `gitrepo`, which already wraps git commands—adding a shared `gitrepo.Version(ctx)` function that both telemetry and strategy could call, though that means telemetry would pick up a new import it currently avoids.

I'm wary of an import cycle though, since gitrepo pulls in logging and other packages. A safer approach might be exporting a pure `telemetry.ParseGitVersion` function that strategy can reuse for comparing major/minor versions, avoiding the need to duplicate parsing logic across packages.

Actually, I could just use `telemetry.GitVersion(ctx)` directly in place of the exec call in readGitCommentConfig, since it already handles timeouts and failure cases gracefully. But I should first check whether a neutral package already exists for this -- maybe something like a dedicated git version helper -- by searching for existing "--version" git checks, and verify that gitrepo doesn't transitively depend on telemetry before deciding where this logic should live.

The git --version call doesn't target a repo, so it's safe, and the 5s timeout fits a hook context. For issue #8, attach running git config twice: I should fix this by wrapping the context with strategy.WithCommentConfig once at the top of runAttach, before planAttachLink, so both calls to FinalCheckpointTrailers share the same snapshot instead of reading config twice.

The explain path's getAssociatedCommits for #2 should get the same WithCommentConfig treatment, and #9 is already handled by #1's design. I want to revisit the risks of #1's prepare-side change for the agent fast path and check existing tests for cases where a message already has a trailer that prepare should preserve.

For the stamped record write, I'm trying to figure out where exactly to place it — likely after the message file is written across the slow path, fast path, and amend restore. I'm considering a helper to record the stamped trailer, and digging into the git history to see what the previous implementation (removed before) was called and why. The prior version acted as a fallback to relink moved trailers, which caused conflicts with attach/explain and matched against commented-out trailers — issues raised in round 3 review. My new approach differs because it's purely a restriction that never adds a link beyond the final block, so it shouldn't reintroduce those disagreements.

Now I'm tracing through attach's logic: it resolves the checkpoint ID from the existing final-block ID and writes the session into that checkpoint. If someone runs attach on a commit made with a teammate's SHA, whether or not that checkpoint has been fetched, attach would write the session into the teammate's checkpoint. I'm weighing whether this matches the reviewer's earlier concern about prepare/post-commit, or whether joining an existing checkpoint via the final block is intentional behavior — since attach is explicitly meant to join whatever checkpoint the commit's final block declares, even if it belongs to someone else.

If that teammate's checkpoint isn't fetched locally, attach would end up creating a brand-new local checkpoint with the same ID, setting up the exact same kind of future conflict seen in that earlier issue. The reviewer hasn't actually flagged this for attach though, so I want to stay within scope rather than widen it, but I should quickly check whether attach fetches first before deciding how to handle a missing local checkpoint — there's a test name that hints it does. I'll look at the actual code now to confirm.

Found that #1 and #9 share a root cause (post-commit writes into the wrong trailer since prepare doesn't record which ID it stamped), plus fixes for #2, #3, and minor ones for #4/#5/#7/#8, with #6 left as a design answer in the PR description. I'll make these fixes locally without pushing, then check the test blast radius next.
